maths:referee.verdict: Sound as mathematics for whole n, but not yet a good picture, and the "forced" story is overstated. My own from-scratch implementation (radial layout) confirms every structural claim to rounding error: independent of the copy, continuous on the whole sphere, exact on z = 0, degree n^2, the three expected branch directions, first-order doubling at A and B->C. Two things the proposal does not say: (1) the simplest layout is a poor choice. It leaves a first-order crease all along the plane z = 0, and on the half plane y = 0, x < 0 squaring degenerates to exactly v -> -|v| v (no angle doubling at all), which grows a thin fin about 2.4 tall in the Mandelbrot solid and makes the x-z slice a fat blob. Off-plane horizontal slices are also still not in one piece. (2) The triangular pillow is singled out only among straight (flat-geodesic) circles, and even then it carries TWO such circles through the fixed corner, not one; choosing the layout so both are laid at constant speed makes the planes z = 0 AND y = 0 both exact and removes the fin (I built and measured this). So: adopt the pillow, but not with the simplest layout, and do not tell the user the rule is unique. confirmed: Claim 1, copy independence: 200,000 random directions, 4 random pillow symmetries composed (shifts by colour-A lattice points, 120 degree turns about arbitrary lattice points). Max difference in Phi(n*u) over all n in -5..8: 5.3e-12 (1.5e-12 for squaring). Control with a non-symmetry (shift by a colour-B point): 1.73, so the test has teeth. Round trip Phi(PhiInv(d)) = d to 2.5e-15.

Claim 1, continuity: scans along 33 great circles (24 random plus near-equator, corner meridians, pole circles with 1e-9 tilts) at 20,000 and 200,000 samples. The largest step shrinks by 9.8 to 10.0 times when sampling is 10 times finer for every n, so there is no jump. Direct straddle tests with offset 1e-10: across the equator the two sides differ by 4e-10 (squaring) to 1.6e-9 (n = 8); across the meridians at 0, 60, 120, 180, 240, 300 degrees by 8e-10 to 4e-9. Images of circles of radius 1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9 around A, B, C, both poles and the three arc midpoints shrink in proportion (worst case 1.6e-8 at radius 1e-9, n = 8).

Claim 1, equator: 1,000,721 angles including every whole degree. Direction error at most 1.2e-14 for all n; full F against the complex power r^n e^(i n phi) has relative error at most 1.2e-14, negative n included.

Claim 2, degree: Fibonacci mesh of 150,000 points, 40 random targets. Exactly n^2 preimages for n = +-1, +-2, +-3 (4 for squaring) with none reversed. For |n| >= 4 the count is n^2 plus k extra with k reversed (signed count consistent with n^2); the extras are mesh triangles straddling creases. Follow-up with 3 million triangles of size 1e-6: 1 reversed for squaring, 6 for n = 8, and mean area stretch 3.9997, 8.998, 24.999, 63.99 for n = 2, 3, 5, 8.

Claim 2, branch directions of squaring: a blind scan of 12,000 centres (winding number of the image of a circle of radius 0.06) found 11,985 ordinary points and 15 anomalous ones in exactly three clusters, at longitude 60.3, 179.7 and 299.9 degrees on the equator. At the exact arc midpoints the winding number is 3.000 at radii 1e-2, 1e-4, 1e-6; at A, B, C and both poles it is 1.000. What happens there: a small disc around the midpoint is wrapped three times around the image corner (60 deg -> B, 180 deg -> A, 300 deg -> C), while the equator itself passes straight through. Also A -> A, B -> C, C -> B, north pole <-> south pole. Three branch points of order 3 is exactly what a degree 4 sphere map needs (2*4 - 2 = 6).

Claim 3: at angle eps from A, the image angle from the x axis divided by eps lies in [2.000, 2.169] at eps = 0.3, [2.000, 2.051] at 0.1, [2.000, 2.0049] at 0.01, [2.000, 2.00049] at 0.001; the angle around the axis changes by at most 3.24, 1.30, 0.14, 0.014 degrees. Identical numbers at B with the image measured about C. So the statement holds to first order (error proportional to eps), not exactly.

Claim 4 inside the pillow: two copies of the same direction that differ by a 120 degree turn about B or C give answers that disagree by a median of 1.5 (max 2.0) after multiplying by 2.5, 1.5 or 2.2; a turn about A gives 0 (3e-15). With the rule exactly as defined and n = 2.5, the arcs A-B and C-A of the equator are exact (2e-15) and continuous, but on the arc B-C (120 to 240 degrees) the image of the equator leaves the plane (|z| up to 0.90), the error against the flat power is up to 2.0, and the two sides of z = 0 disagree by up to 1.81.

Claim 5, the two circles: enumerating all 172 primitive straight directions through corner A with lattice coordinates up to 14, exactly 12 close up without self-crossing. They are the 6 edge directions (length 3, one circle through A, B, C) and the 6 altitude directions (length sqrt 3, one circle through A, both face centres and the midpoint of B-C). On the second circle (the great circle y = 0) squaring is exactly doubling in the flat parameter (4e-16) and the circle is invariant (|y| < 3e-15).

Claim 5, square pillow about a face centre: for n = 3, 5, 7, -3 it is independent of the copy (2.5e-13), continuous (step ratio 9.3 to 10.4), exact on z = 0 (8e-15) AND on y = 0 (5e-15), symmetric under a quarter turn about the x axis (1.4e-14), with mean area stretch 9.00, 24.99, 49.00, 9.00. Side check: the angle-true (conformal) version of the pillow squaring is the classical rational map w -> (2w^3 - 1)/(w(2 - w^3)) in the usual sphere coordinate w = (x+iy)/(1-z). Checked: it is the doubling formula of the Weierstrass P' function of the colour-A lattice (lattice-sum relative error 5e-6 to 4e-5), fixes 1, swaps the other cube roots of 1, sends -1 to 1 with a triple root, keeps the unit circle, and on it doubles the angle with a wobble of up to 60.0 degrees.
wrong_or_unproven: Layout defect 1, crease on z = 0 (not mentioned in the proposal). With the radial layout the longitude of F_2 picks up a term proportional to |latitude| with the same sign above and below the plane: measured slopes +0.4445, +1.1113, -0.4445, +1.1113 at longitudes 20, 50, 100, 170 degrees, matching my formula (8/3)(p - k) where p is the position along the 120 degree arc. So F is continuous but not differentiable across z = 0; expect a ridge line where the solid crosses the plane. It vanishes only if the layout's lines of constant longitude leave the triangle edges at right angles (I derived this condition; the radial layout violates it everywhere except at the corners).

Layout defect 2, the fin. On the half plane y = 0, x < 0 the radial layout turns squaring into exactly v -> -|v| v (error 2.5e-15): the direction is flipped, not doubled. On the circle y = 0 the map deviates from doubling by up to 90 degrees. Consequence: the x-z slice of the Mandelbrot solid is a blob of area 3.81 (flat set 1.655; 202,244 pixels differ) that runs off the +-1.3 box, and the solid has a thin vertical fin, which is why its z extent (1.20) exceeds its width. 'Expands everywhere, nothing attracts' is true only in the pillow's own flat measure; on the round sphere the stretch along this circle is 2, 4, 4, 1 and the overall stretch bound for squaring is about 6.8, not 2.

The claim that the result matches Figure 4 is unproven. My slices of the pillow solid are feathery and dusty away from z = 0 (see slice_pillow_z0.10.png, slice_pillow_z0.25.png, slice_pillow_x-0.5_yz.png), not round bodies with beads. The user's original complaint (off-plane slices disconnected and odd looking) is reduced but not removed: 93.5 / 85.0 / 69.2% in one piece. Whether the 3D solid is truly connected cannot be decided from a grid; 99.2% in one piece is at the level of sampling crumbs.

Uniqueness as stated is too strong, see the uniqueness field: two circles on the triangular pillow, an open case for non-straight circles, and a free choice of layout that changes the picture more than anything else.

Claim 4 as a general impossibility statement is false. Topologically a rule that is exact on z = 0 and discontinuous only on the negative x axis exists (extend the angle function constantly along the circles through (-1,0,0) that cross the equator at right angles), though it is not a pillow rule and would be badly distorted near that axis. I did not implement it. Within the pillow rule as proposed the claim is right, for a precise reason: B and C are passed straight through by the unrolled equator, and each side of the plane near them has three copies that fractional scaling tells apart, so a seam must leave the rays through B and C on both sides of the plane or lie in the plane itself.

Untested: on the same pillow turned so that the altitude circle is the plane z = 0, the only gluing that fractional scaling breaks is the edge B-C, which then stands upright over the negative x axis and meets z = 0 only there, the same cut as the flat fractional power. Derived on paper, not run.

'Smooth near the corner directions' is too generous. F is differentiable AT A, B, C (derivative 2 times identity, per claim 3) but creased along the equator and the corner meridians arbitrarily close to them.

I did not check that the pillow map with an angle-true layout equals the rational map numerically (that needs the Schwarz triangle map); it follows from standard theory plus the checks listed. Kucera's own 3D construction is omitted from the paper, so the link to it is by structure, not by reproducing his set.
maths:referee.uniqueness: What holds: if the invariant circle is required to be a straight line of the flat pillow (equivalently, any curve of finite length), the argument is short. The circle carries one fixed point of the doubling, and there the map must stretch by +2 with no turn; on all four pillows the only fixed points with that property are corners. A straight line through a corner of even order (2, 4, 6) is folded back on itself, so the corner must have order 3. That leaves (3,3,3) and the order-3 corner of (2,3,6); on (2,3,6) squaring acts at that corner as multiplication by -2, which reverses the circle. So (2,2,2,2), (2,4,4) and (2,3,6) are out for squaring, including the versions with multipliers 2i and other norm-4 multipliers, and on (3,3,3) the multiplier must be +2 (the -2 version fixes all three corners and gives the conjugate-squaring, i.e. tricorn, rule). What does not hold: (a) the triangular pillow has two such circles through the fixed corner, the edge circle (proposed, corners at the cube roots of 1 in the plane) and the altitude circle (through A, the two face centres and the midpoint of B-C); my enumeration of 172 directions found exactly these two. The proposal silently picks one. (b) I cannot exclude wild, infinitely wiggly invariant circles on the other pillows; I doubt they matter but it is not proved. (c) The wrapping of the pillow onto the sphere is a whole function's worth of freedom and it decides whether the result has a fin, a crease, or a second exact plane. (d) For odd n the square pillow about a face centre is a genuine second rule (confirmed for 3, 5, 7, -3; two perpendicular exact planes, quarter-turn symmetry about the x axis); for even n it does not exist. Honest wording for the user: squaring forces the three special directions and removes the 'number of planes' dial, but it does not force one unique rule.
maths:referee.kucera_link: Same skeleton, different flesh. Kucera's generators meet the unit sphere exactly at A = 1 and the other two cube roots of 1, with A fixed and B, C swapped; the pillow's corners are those points with the same behaviour (checked). His two-generator group has only the unit circle as limit set and gives the 'inflated' set; the plain Riemann-sphere rule is the exact counterpart (its direction map is chaotic only on the equator), and my measurement shows the same character: a smooth lens only 0.26 thick whose slices are single blobs. His third generator g3 is g2 turned 90 degrees about the x axis; it makes the whole unit sphere the limit set. The pillow is the counterpart of that step: its direction map is chaotic on the whole sphere (in its angle-true form it is the classical rational map w -> (2w^3-1)/(w(2-w^3)), whose restriction to the equator is an approximate doubling with a wobble, the same kind of curve Kucera plots in Figure 2 right, and the layout is what straightens it to exact doubling). A further match: g3's spheres touch g1's sphere at (-1/2, 0, +-sqrt3/2), and those are exactly where the both-planes-exact layout puts the pillow's two face centres, so his 3D set and that variant both carry the flat set in the two perpendicular planes through the real axis (consistent with his restriction to real c). But the pillow is not his construction: his map is pieced together from sphere inversions and is unpublished in detail; the pillow is a different explicit map with the same combinatorics. The 'use the third map' checkbox: it is the same idea (add a generator at right angles so the action spreads into the third direction), which is precisely Kucera's step from the inflated to the truly 3D picture, but it lives only in Kleinian mode. Mandelbrot and Julia modes have no group and no generator to switch on, so the button cannot fix them and should not be wired to them; the pillow is that idea rebuilt for power maps. Quaternions do not force anything here either: quaternion squaring only spins the flat set about the real axis (the paper calls it trivial).
maths:referee.plain_text:
The new rule holds up. I rebuilt it from the description and tested every whole power from -5 to 8: there are no tears anywhere, and the flat slice at z = 0 matches the ordinary 2D picture pixel for pixel. So the seams that made the current "two planes" version fall apart are gone, and there is no "number of planes" dial any more. Three special directions do the job, and squaring itself picks them.

Two honest warnings. First, the simplest way of wrapping the pillow onto the ball gives an ugly solid: a tall thin fin standing on the real axis, a faint ridge along z = 0, and off-plane slices that are still dusty (93, 85 and 69 percent in one piece at heights 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5). A better wrapping that I tried makes the upright slice an exact Mandelbrot set too and removes the fin. Second, the "third map" checkbox only affects Kleinian mode. It is the same idea, but it cannot be reused here.
alternatives: Both-planes-exact pillow (measured, recommended over the radial layout). Same Phi and PhiInv, but after the layout slide each direction with z >= 0 along the half circle through (0,+-1,0): tau = atan2(z, x), tau' = (4/3) tau for tau <= 90 deg, else (2/3) tau + 60 deg, keep y, set (x, z) = hypot(x, z) * (cos tau', sin tau'); apply the inverse slide before the inverse layout. Face centres land at (-1/2, 0, +-sqrt3/2). Result: z = 0 and y = 0 both exact, fin gone, z extent 0.85 against 0.88 in y, slices 96.6 / 97.9 / 87.6% in one piece. It gives up the 120 degree cycling symmetry and has a kink at tau = 90 deg that should be smoothed.

Which circle is the floor: a toggle that swaps y and z in the both-planes-exact variant. This is the 'side-on pillow': A at (1,0,0), face centres at +-120 deg on the equator, B and C above and below the plane. Same map, different exact floor plan relative to the corners, and (untested) a natural single cut for fractional powers in the upright plane over the negative x axis.

Crease-free layout. Requirement: lines of constant longitude meet the triangle edges at right angles. Candidate in the sub-triangle nearest an edge, with xi = foot of the perpendicular on that edge (0..1), m = smallest weight, r = (xi - 1.5 m)/(1 - 3 m) the radial edge parameter: use p = r + (xi - r) * B with B = (xi - 1.5 m)(1 - 1.5 m - xi)/(xi (1 - xi)); longitude from p as before, latitude from m as before. It has zero normal derivative at the edge and agrees with the radial layout on the corner rays; it still needs a check that it stays one-to-one.

Angle-true pillow in closed form: direction map w -> (2w^3 - 1)/(w(2 - w^3)) with w = (x + i y)/(1 - z). No triangles, no creases, very cheap in a shader, chaotic on the whole sphere. It breaks the standing requirement (the plane z = 0 is kept but the angle is doubled with a wobble of up to 60 degrees), so offer it only as a labelled 'smooth, not exact' reference to see what the pillow looks like without layout artefacts.

Square pillow for odd powers (3, 5, 7, -3 confirmed): two unit squares sewn along their edges, face centre at (1,0,0), the square's rim on the great circle x = 0, multiply by n about the face centre. Two perpendicular exact planes and quarter-turn symmetry about the x axis. Not available for even n.
Tricorn for free: |v|^2 * Phi(-2 * PhiInv(v/|v|)). On z = 0 this is exactly conjugate-squaring (the equator check for the n = -2 direction map passed at 4e-15), and all three corners are fixed.

proto:twoplane.summary: Built the pillow approach with the layout "radial from the altitude's midpoint" (id "pillow", first in APPROACHES, GLSL plus JavaScript mirror, no dials) and ran all five checks and all standard pictures in 43 minutes. The rule is correct: both planes z = 0 and y = 0 follow the complex power to 7e-15, it is continuous everywhere tested, and the shader matches the JavaScript. The pictures are bad. The solids are fibrous and creased all over: the basilica is three pointed, ridged bodies (a diamond seen along x), the Mandelbrot solid is a lump of feathered sheets, and there are no round bodies and no beads, so it looks nothing like Figure 4. The cause is measurable: because O is off-centre the direction map is very lopsided (s1/s2 median 3.2, 95th percentile 14.3, worst 33.6 at n = 2). Sliced off the plane the solid stays mostly in one piece (largest piece 94.8% to 100%) but frays into specks. My verdict: this layout should not ship; its one real gain is the second exact plane.
proto:twoplane.formulas:
F_n(v) = |v|^k * Phi(k * PhiInv(v/|v|)), k = floor(n + 1/2). F(0) = 0 for k > 0; lengths capped at e^42 like the other approaches; origin under a negative power -> (e^42, 0, 0). Flat positions are kept in lattice coordinates (a, b) = the point a*(1,0) + b*(-1/2, sqrt(3)/2); scaling by k is the same in either system. T = 2*pi/3.

PhiInv(d), d a unit direction:
  s = atan2(hypot(d.x, d.y), |d.z|) / (pi/2)        (share of the way from the pole O to the equator)
  t = atan2(d.y, d.x) / T; if t < 0: t += 3          (equator position in thirds: 0 at A, 1 at B, 2 at C)
  k3 = min(floor(t), 2); f = t - k3
  (qB, qC) = (f, 0) if k3 = 0; (1 - f, f) if k3 = 1; (0, 1 - f) if k3 = 2     (where the ray from O ends on the boundary)
  lB = 1/4 + s*(qB - 1/4); lC = 1/4 + s*(qC - 1/4)    (lA = 1 - lB - lC; O has weights 1/2, 1/4, 1/4)
  (a, b) = (lB, -lC) if d.z >= 0, else (lB + lC, lC)   (same as u = lB*(1,0) + lC*(1/2, -+sqrt(3)/2))

Phi(a, b):
  i = floor(a), j = floor(b), fa = a - i, fb = b - j
  w0 = 1 - max(fa, fb); w1 = |fa - fb|; w2 = min(fa, fb); c0 = (i + j) mod 3 (taken as 0, 1 or 2)
  (lA, lB, lC) = (w0, w1, w2) if c0 = 0; (w2, w0, w1) if c0 = 1; (w1, w2, w0) if c0 = 2
  sigma = -1 if fa >= fb (triangle points up: lower half sphere), else +1
  m = min(2*lA, 4*lB, 4*lC); s = 1 - m; if s is 0 (below 1e-12 in JS, 1e-6 in GLSL): return (0, 0, sigma)
  t = 1/4 + (lB - 1/4)/s if 4*lC is the least (ray leaves through edge AB);
  t = 5/4 + (lC - 1/4)/s else if 2*lA is the least (edge BC);
  t = 5/2 + (lA - 1/2)/s otherwise (edge CA)
  phi = T*t; e = (pi/2)*m; return (cos e * cos phi, cos e * sin phi, sigma * sin e)
(theta = (pi/2)*(1 - m) is the exactly linear polar angle; writing it with m keeps a zero weight exactly on the equator.)

Added to make it work, without changing the rule: exactly on z = 0 (v.z == 0) the complex power is taken directly in both JS and GLSL (same value, checked against the general path; it stops round-off lifting orbits off the plane, which this everywhere-expanding rule would amplify up to about 4x per step); sqr uses |v|^2 directly. mul(a, b) of two different points, cmap (identity), aprDiv and aprSPow are copied from the sphere-inversion approach (aprMmul without folds), and the approach's "about" text says so. In the shader c0 is computed as sum - 3*floor((sum + 0.5)/3) to be safe against float division. proto:radial.summary: I built the pillow rule with the "radial from the centre" layout as approach id "pillow", first entry of out/proto/radial/10-approaches.js (GLSL plus JavaScript mirror, no dials), on the test page dist/proto-radial.html. Every numeric check passes: exact on z = 0 to 7e-15 with the z part exactly 0, continuous everywhere, shader matches JavaScript. The pictures are not good and I would not ship this layout. The solid is one fat lump with a fibrous, shredded surface; it does not look like Kucera's Figure 4 (no lemon bodies, no rows of beads). Shape distortion is large for every profile I tried (best variant: median stretch ratio 2.56, 95th percentile 6.0, ideal 1), because the shear is built into laying the triangle out along rays from its centre. The flat set is also fragile: by z = 0.02 the Mandelbrot disc and needle have merged into a wedge, so the 3D cut face "at height 0" does not show the crisp flat set. The final version uses an equal-area profile with rounded level curves; the two rejected variants (plain q(s) = s, and equal area without rounding) are in out/proto/radial/rejected/. Time used: 44 minutes (22:02 to 22:46).
proto:radial.formulas:
Final version (equal-area profile, rounded level curves). T3 = 2*pi/3.

LAYOUT, weights (lA, lB, lC) -> unit direction with z >= 0:
  mn = min(lA, lB, lC); e = 3*mn; s = 1 - e   (s = 0 centre, 1 boundary)
  k = 0 if lC <= lA and lC <= lB (edge AB); else 1 if lA <= lB (edge BC); else 2 (edge CA)
  next = lB, lC, lA for k = 0, 1, 2; t = clamp((next - mn)/s, 0, 1), or 1/2 when s = 0
  w = 2t - 1; lam = sqrt(1 + 3*w*w)
  eps = e / (1 + s*(lam - 1))   (the rounding; without it eps = e)
  z = eps*(2 - eps); rho = (1 - eps)*sqrt(1 + z); tau = T3*(k + t)
  direction = (rho*cos(tau), rho*sin(tau), z)
  (rejected profile "lin": z = sin(pi/2*eps), rho = cos(pi/2*eps))

INVERSE, (x, y, z >= 0) -> weights:
  eps = z / (1 + sqrt(1 - z))   ("lin": eps = asin(z)*2/pi)
  a = atan2(y, x)/T3 (0 at the pole), plus 3 if negative; k = min(floor(a), 2); t = a - k
  w = 2t - 1; lam = sqrt(1 + 3*w*w); e = lam*eps / (1 + eps*(lam - 1))   (without rounding e = eps)
  m = (1-t, t, 0), (0, 1-t, t), (t, 0, 1-t) for k = 0, 1, 2; l = e/3 + (1 - e)*m

RULE F_n(v), with m = round(n), r = |v|:
  m = 0 -> (1, 0, 0). r < 1e-20 -> (0,0,0) if m > 0, else (aprPow(r, m), 0, 0).
  d = v/r; l = INVERSE(d.x, d.y, |d.z|)
  X = l if d.z >= 0, else (lA + lC, lB + lC, -lC)   (mirror image in edge AB)
  Y = (m*XA - (m - 1), m*XB, m*XC)   (times m about corner A; a negative m includes the half turn)
  i = floor(Y); f = Y - i; S = fA + fB + fC; colour k = (iB - iC) mod 3
  g = (1, 0, 0) if S < 0.5 or S >= 2.5 (exactly on a lattice point)
    = (1 - fA, 1 - fC, 1 - fB) if 1.5 < S < 2.5 (upside-down triangle, lower half sphere: flip)
    = (fA, fB, fC) otherwise
  weights[(k + j) mod 3] = g[j] for j = 0, 1, 2; D = LAYOUT(weights); if flip, D.z = -D.z
  F = aprPow(r, m) * D   (the lab's capped power, lengths stop at e^42)

(XA, XB, XC) are the weights of the triangle with A at the origin, continued linearly over the sheet; the task's lattice coordinates are (a, b) = (XB, -XC). Using three coordinates keeps a zero weight exactly zero on all three edges, so a point of z = 0 returns z = 0 exactly, in the shader too. In GLSL the colour is k = mod(iB - iC + 0.5, 3.0) tested against 1.0 and 2.0. pw and sqr use this rule; mul of two different points, cmap, aprDiv and aprSPow are copied from Sphere inversions with one plane (the approach text says so), so mul(v, v) is not the pillow square.

proto:sine.summary: Built the pillow rule with the "barycentric sines" layout as approach id "pillow" (first entry, no dials) in out/proto/sine/10-approaches.js, with a JavaScript mirror and GLSL, and a private page dist/proto-sine.html. Lift chosen: equal-area (z = 1 - |H|^2), after comparing eight lifts numerically; orthographic was rejected because it has unbounded stretch. All five numeric checks pass after one real fault was found and fixed (this GPU's cos() and asin() are only good to 4-5 digits, which made the shader differ from JavaScript by 2e-4 to 3e-3 until I rewrote the layout with half-angle sines and a corrected asin). Honest verdict on the pictures: z = 0 is the flat set, there are no seams or jumps, and off the plane the solid stays mostly in one piece (largest piece 94-100 % of the solid, a few small detached islands at heights 0.25 and 0.5). But it does NOT look like Kucera's Figure 4: the Mandelbrot solid is a flame-like mass of fins, the basilica is one lumpy body rather than a row of lemon bodies, and there are no bead rows. The flat set sits at the bottom of a groove along z = 0 (the slice at 0.2 is a fat oval, much bigger than the basilica), and the map is creased there and stretches unevenly (median stretch ratio 2.0, ideal 1.0). Both faults come from the layout formula, not the lift, so this assignment's free choices cannot fix them; no second layout version was made. About 45 minutes used.
proto:sine.formulas:
F_n(v) = |v|^k * Phi(k * PhiInv(v/|v|)), k = round(n) (also used for the length, through aprPow, capped at e^42). k = 1 returns v. |v| < 1e-20 with k > 0 returns 0. If the input z is exactly 0 the output z is set to exactly 0 (the snap).

LAYOUT (weights lA, lB, lC; T = 2*pi/3; eA, eB, eC unit vectors at 0, 120, 240 degrees):
  H = (2/sqrt3) * (sin(T lA) eA + sin(T lB) eB + sin(T lC) eC)
  lift (equal-area): z = q = 1 - |H|^2, (x, y) = H * sqrt(1 + z); negate z for a bottom (pointing-up) triangle.
Evaluated from the heaviest corner: cyclically turn the weights so the heaviest is first (m = its position among colours k, k+1, k+2), call the other two w1 (next colour) and w2, and with sb = sin(T w1/2), sg = sin(T w2/2), cb = sqrt(1 - sb^2), cg = sqrt(1 - sg^2):
  S = sb cg + cb sg; C = cb cg - sb sg; D = (2/sqrt3) sb sg
  Hx = 1 - 2 S (S + D); Hy = 2 C (sb cg - cb sg); q = 4 sb sg (4 C^2 cb cg + (2/sqrt3) S (1 - 2 S^2 - S D))
then turn (Hx, Hy) by 120 degrees times the heaviest corner's colour c = (k + m) mod 3. Same H as above, written as products so q is exactly 0 on an edge.

Phi(u): b = 2 u.y/sqrt3, a = u.x + b/2, i = floor(a), j = floor(b), fa = a - i, fb = b - j, k = (i + j) mod 3. If fa >= fb (points up, bottom, z <= 0) the weights of colours k, k+1, k+2 are (1 - fa, fa - fb, fb); otherwise (points down, top) they are (1 - fb, fb - fa, fa).

PhiInv(d): q = |d.z|; H = d.xy / sqrt(1 + |d.z|). If |Hy| > sqrt3 * Hx set c = 1 (Hy > 0) or 2 and turn H by -120*c degrees; else c = 0. Then
  T0 = (Hy^2 + q)/(1 + Hx); p = min(sqrt(T0/2), 0.8)
  Newton on f(p) = 2p^2 + (2/sqrt3) p (cc - ss) - T0, with ss = sqrt(1 - p^2), e = Hy^2/(4 ss^2), cc = sqrt(max(1 - e, 1e-12)), f'(p) = 4p + (2/sqrt3)((cc - ss) + p^2 (1/ss - e/(cc ss^2))); p = clamp(p - f/max(f', 1e-20), 0, 0.8). JavaScript 4 steps, shader 3 (measured flat error after 1/2/3/4 steps: 4.6e-3, 2.1e-5, 4.7e-10, 3.5e-16).
  sh = asin(p); th = asin(clamp(Hy/(2 ss), -p, p)); w1 = (sh + th)/T; w2 = (sh - th)/T; w0 = 1 - w1 - w2
  (lA, lB, lC) = (w0, w1, w2) for c = 0, (w2, w0, w1) for c = 1, (w1, w2, w0) for c = 2
  u = lB*(1, 0) + lC*(1/2, -sqrt3/2) if d.z >= 0, else lB*(1, 0) + lC*(1/2, +sqrt3/2).

Shader only: asin is replaced by pilAsin(x) = y - (sin(y) - x) * inversesqrt(1 - sin(y)^2) with y = asin(x), valid for |x| <= 0.8, and no cos() is called anywhere, because this GPU's cos and asin are inexact.

mul(a, b) and cmap are the sphere-inversion approach's with one plane (aprMmul copied as pilMul; cmap is the identity). sqr(v) = pw(v, 2).
checks: 1. Exactness on z = 0 (JavaScript rule vs complex power, 500 points per n: 300 random, 160 within 1e-9..1e-1 of 0/120/180/240 degrees, 40 with radius 1e-6..1e-1). Worst relative error: n=2 1.84e-15, n=3 5.10e-15, n=4 3.73e-15, n=5 6.44e-15, n=8 7.09e-15, n=-1 8.23e-16, n=-2 1.99e-15, n=-3 4.04e-15. PASS (limit 1e-6). With the snap switched off the output |z| is at most 5.4e-15 of its length, so the snap hides nothing in double precision.

2. Continuity (200000 random pairs of unit directions 1e-5 apart + 74000 special pairs across the equator, across the six meridians through corners and mid-edges, at poles, corners and mid-edges). Largest ratio / 99.9th percentile / median: n=2 4.022 / 4.005 / 2.220; n=3 9.054 / 9.008 / 3.174; n=-2 4.019 / 4.003 / 2.218. PASS, no jump. The largest values equal n^2 and sit on the equator beside the corner directions (0, 120, 240 degrees).

3. Round trips. Phi(PhiInv(d)) - d over 260000 directions (random plus next to equator, corners, mid-edges, poles, meridians): worst 1.60e-15. PhiInv(Phi(u)) vs u over 200000 flat points (a quarter within 1e-3 of a lattice point): worst weight difference 4.44e-16; wrong triangle type away from an edge: 0. PASS.

4. Shader vs JavaScript (float texture, 12800 points per power in five regions: anywhere, on the plane, beside corners and mid-edges, beside poles, beside the plane). Worst relative difference: n=2 2.1e-6, n=3 3.2e-6, n=4 4.5e-6, n=5 5.5e-6, n=8 7.9e-6, n=-1 1.4e-6, n=-2 2.8e-6, n=-3 3.1e-6; medians 2.3e-7 to 1.4e-6. On the plane the shader's z is exactly 0 and x, y are within 1.3e-6 (n=2) to 4.8e-6 (n=8) of the complex power. sqr(v) vs pw(v,2): 7.1e-6 absolute; pw(v,1) = v exactly; all results finite at origin, axes, corners, 1e18 (largest component 1.74e18).
